I. PURPOSE

This framework is designed for the real-world analysis of human claims, arguments, debates, evidence, reasoning, scientific claims, mathematical claims, causal claims, computational claims, strategic claims, and related questions.

The framework uses 18 selected real-world analytical domains.

The 18-domain structure is a framework selected for this project. It is not being claimed to be an official or universally accepted classification of exactly 18 disciplines.

Each domain must be used according to its actual definitions, methods, assumptions, evidence requirements, and scope.

Mathematics, science, logic, evidence, statistics, and the other domains are not literal weapons, shields, forces, or fictional abilities.

II. PRIMARY TARGET

Primary real-world target:

HUMAN ARGUMENT + DEBATE + CLAIMS + EVIDENCE + REASONING

The framework evaluates the claim or argument itself.

A claim does not become true merely because it is confidently stated, repeated, popular, persuasive, or supported by an authority.

Likewise, a claim does not become false merely because it is unpopular, difficult to understand, or challenged.

The actual evidence and reasoning must be evaluated.

III. FICTION AND REAL-WORLD EVIDENCE

Fictional works may contain fictional statements, characters, events, abilities, rules, and worlds.

FICTIONAL CLAIM != REAL-WORLD EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE

A fictional statement does not automatically become evidence about the physical real world merely because it appears in an anime, manga, comic, novel, game, SCP story, or other fictional work.

If fictional material is discussed, it must remain identified as fictional material rather than silently being converted into real-world scientific evidence.

IV. 18-DOMAIN INDEX

  1. Mathematics
  2. Formal Logic
  3. Probability & Statistics
  4. Information Theory
  5. Computation Theory
  6. Optimization
  7. Dimensional Analysis
  8. Science
  9. Scientific Methodology
  10. Measurement & Metrology
  11. Causality
  12. Systems Theory

1. MATHEMATICS

Mathematics studies abstract structures, quantities, relationships, patterns, and formal consequences.

Mathematical proof establishes conclusions from specified definitions, axioms, assumptions, and rules of inference.

MATHEMATICAL PROOF != EMPIRICAL PHYSICAL EVIDENCE

A mathematical result can establish what follows within the specified mathematical framework.

It does not, by itself, establish that a mathematical model accurately describes a physical system.

MATHEMATICAL MODEL != PHYSICAL REALITY

2. FORMAL LOGIC

Formal Logic studies formally structured reasoning and logical consequence.

It can evaluate:

  • Premises
  • Conclusions
  • Inference
  • Validity
  • Logical consequence
  • Consistency
  • Formal proof
  • Satisfiability
VALIDITY != TRUTH OF PREMISES

A formally valid argument can have false premises.

Therefore, evaluating an argument requires distinguishing:

  • the logical relationship between premises and conclusion;
  • whether the premises are true or otherwise acceptable;
  • whether available evidence supports the premises.

3. PROBABILITY & STATISTICS

Probability and Statistics concern uncertainty, variation, data, statistical relationships, estimation, and inference.

Relevant concepts include:

  • Probability
  • Random variables
  • Probability distributions
  • Sampling
  • Estimation
  • Statistical inference
  • Statistical models
  • Data analysis
  • Uncertainty
POSSIBILITY != PROBABILITY
PROBABILITY != CERTAINTY

A probability claim must be interpreted according to its definitions, model, assumptions, data, and context.

Statistical conclusions must be evaluated according to the method used and its assumptions.

4. INFORMATION THEORY

Information Theory mathematically studies information, uncertainty, communication, coding, and related quantities.

Relevant concepts include:

  • Entropy
  • Information measures
  • Coding
  • Compression
  • Communication channels
  • Noise
  • Channel capacity

Technical information quantities must not automatically be treated as equivalent to knowledge, truth, meaning, or intelligence.

INFORMATION != AUTOMATICALLY KNOWLEDGE
INFORMATION != AUTOMATICALLY TRUTH

Claims involving "infinite information" require a precise definition and mathematical context.

5. COMPUTATION THEORY

Computation Theory studies formal computation and its limits.

Relevant concepts include:

  • Algorithms
  • Computability
  • Computational models
  • Decidability
  • Complexity
  • Computational limits
COMPUTABILITY != PRACTICAL FEASIBILITY

A problem may be computable while being impractical under a particular resource constraint.

Claims of computational impossibility require a specified computational model and a definition of what "impossible" means.

6. OPTIMIZATION

Optimization studies maximum, minimum, optimal, or extremal solutions under specified objectives and constraints.

A meaningful optimization problem requires relevant elements such as:

  • Objective
  • Variables
  • Domain
  • Constraints
  • Feasible solutions
  • Optimization criterion

"BEST" or "MAXIMUM" requires a defined problem and comparison criterion.

An undefined domain does not establish an absolute maximum.

7. DIMENSIONAL ANALYSIS

Dimensional Analysis examines relationships between physical quantities and their dimensions.

Examples include:

  • Length
  • Time
  • Mass
  • Velocity
  • Acceleration
  • Force
  • Energy
DIMENSIONAL CONSISTENCY != COMPLETE PHYSICAL VALIDITY

A dimensionally consistent equation can still be physically incorrect.

Dimensional analysis alone does not establish the complete physical mechanism or empirical correctness of an equation.

8. SCIENCE

Science investigates aspects of the natural world using appropriate empirical and theoretical methods.

Scientific work can involve:

  • Observation
  • Measurement
  • Experimentation
  • Modeling
  • Prediction
  • Testing
  • Data analysis
  • Statistical analysis
  • Evidence
  • Reproducibility where applicable

A claim does not become scientific merely because the word "scientific" is attached to it.

The actual evidence, method, assumptions, measurements, models, and limitations must be evaluated.

SCIENCE != AUTOMATIC ABSOLUTE CERTAINTY

9. SCIENTIFIC METHODOLOGY

Scientific Methodology concerns methods used to investigate, test, analyze, evaluate, and revise scientific claims.

Depending on the field and research question, methods may include:

  • Observation
  • Hypothesis formation
  • Prediction
  • Experiment
  • Testing
  • Measurement
  • Data analysis
  • Modeling
  • Statistical reasoning
  • Replication or reproducibility where applicable
  • Critical evaluation
  • Revision

There is not one rigid procedure that must be performed identically in every scientific investigation.

The appropriate method depends on the scientific question, field, available evidence, and relevant constraints.

10. MEASUREMENT & METROLOGY

Metrology is the science of measurement.

Measurement analysis can involve:

  • Measurand
  • Quantity
  • Unit
  • Reference
  • Measurement procedure
  • Calibration
  • Traceability
  • Measurement uncertainty
  • Measurement conditions
  • Fitness for purpose

A numerical value by itself does not necessarily provide all information needed to interpret a measurement.

Measurement results must be understood together with the relevant measurand, unit, method, conditions, and uncertainty.

METROLOGICAL TRACEABILITY

Metrological traceability concerns a measurement result's relationship to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, with each contribution to measurement uncertainty considered.

TRACEABILITY != AUTOMATIC FITNESS FOR PURPOSE

Traceability alone does not guarantee that measurement uncertainty is sufficiently small for a particular purpose.

It also does not automatically guarantee absence of mistakes.

Measurement results must therefore be evaluated according to the requirements of their intended use.

11. CAUSALITY

Causality concerns cause-and-effect relationships.

A claim such as:

"A caused B"

requires appropriate causal support.

Depending on the question, relevant considerations can include:

  • Temporal relationships
  • Mechanisms
  • Confounding
  • Alternative causes
  • Interventions
  • Causal models
  • Relevant evidence
CORRELATION != CAUSATION

A correlation can be relevant to causal investigation, but correlation alone does not establish causation.

12. SYSTEMS THEORY

Systems Theory studies systems and relationships among their components.

Relevant concepts can include:

  • Components
  • Relationships
  • Inputs
  • Outputs
  • Feedback
  • Dependencies
  • Boundaries
  • Interactions
  • Time scales
  • System-level behavior

A systems claim must identify the relevant system, components, relationships, assumptions, and boundaries.

Statements such as:

"Everything affects everything"

are not sufficient by themselves to establish a specific systems relationship.

13. EVIDENCE & EVIDENTIAL REASONING

Evidence is information that can support, challenge, or evaluate a claim.

Evidence evaluation can consider:

  • Relevance
  • Reliability
  • Quality
  • Provenance
  • Context
  • Independence where relevant
  • Alternative explanations
  • Inferential connection
  • Strength of support
SOURCE != AUTOMATIC PROOF

A source may provide evidence without automatically proving every conclusion drawn from it.

The correct question is:

"WHAT EXACTLY DOES THIS EVIDENCE SUPPORT?"

The conclusion must not be stronger than the evidence and reasoning justify.

14. EPISTEMOLOGY

Epistemology studies questions concerning knowledge, belief, justification, evidence, rational support, sources of knowledge, limits of knowledge, and epistemic certainty.

JUSTIFICATION != AUTOMATIC TRUTH
EVIDENCE != AUTOMATIC KNOWLEDGE
NOT PROVEN != PROVEN FALSE

A claim may be justified to some degree without being guaranteed true.

Knowledge claims therefore require appropriate epistemic analysis rather than simply assuming that evidence creates absolute certainty.

15. DECISION THEORY

Decision Theory studies choices under specified conditions involving actions, outcomes, uncertainty, preferences, or objectives.

Relevant elements can include:

  • Available actions
  • Possible outcomes
  • Probabilities or beliefs
  • Preferences
  • Utilities
  • Risks
  • Objectives
  • Information
  • Constraints

"BEST DECISION" is meaningful only relative to a specified decision problem and criterion.

BEST DECISION = DEFINED OBJECTIVE + RELEVANT CONDITIONS + APPLICABLE DECISION CRITERION

16. GAME THEORY

Game Theory studies strategic interactions among agents.

Relevant elements include:

  • Players
  • Actions
  • Strategies
  • Information
  • Rules
  • Timing
  • Preferences
  • Payoffs
  • Outcomes

A claim of "guaranteed victory" requires a sufficiently specified strategic situation.

Rules, players, information, available strategies, timing, objectives, and payoffs must be considered where relevant.

A strategy cannot be called universally winning without specifying the game and conditions.

17. CRITICAL THINKING

Critical Thinking evaluates claims, evidence, reasoning, assumptions, alternatives, and conclusions.

CORE QUESTIONS:

  1. What exactly is the claim?
  2. What do the important terms mean?
  3. What are the premises?
  4. What assumptions are being made?
  5. What evidence exists?
  6. Is the evidence relevant?
  7. Is the evidence reliable?
  8. Does the inference support the conclusion?
  9. Are calculations correct?
  10. Are measurements adequately defined?
  11. Is uncertainty relevant?
  12. Are alternative explanations relevant?
  13. Is the correct discipline being applied?
  14. Is the conclusion stronger than the available support?

18. INFORMAL LOGIC & ARGUMENTATION THEORY

Informal Logic studies reasoning and inference as they occur in public discussion, debate, education, intellectual pursuits, interpersonal exchanges, law, medicine, and other real-life contexts.

It can involve:

  • Argument identification
  • Argument reconstruction
  • Premises
  • Conclusions
  • Inference
  • Evidence
  • Argument evaluation
  • Argument schemes
  • Fallacies
  • Objections
  • Counterarguments
  • Burden of proof
  • Argumentative context

Informal Logic is distinct from Formal Logic because it focuses on arguments as they occur in natural-language and real-life contexts rather than only formally structured languages.

Argumentation Theory is broader and interdisciplinary. It can bring together logical, rhetorical, and dialectical perspectives on real-life arguing.

PERSUASIVENESS != TRUTH

An argument can be persuasive without being adequately supported.

FALLACY != AUTOMATICALLY FALSE CONCLUSION

Identifying a fallacy is part of argument evaluation. It does not by itself establish that the conclusion is false.

There is no single universally agreed taxonomy containing every fallacy. Therefore, fallacy labels must be applied carefully and in context.

V. CORE FACT-BASED DISTINCTIONS

MATHEMATICAL PROOF != EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE
FORMAL VALIDITY != TRUTH OF PREMISES
POSSIBILITY != PROBABILITY
PROBABILITY != CERTAINTY
CORRELATION != CAUSATION
SOURCE != AUTOMATIC PROOF
EVIDENCE != AUTOMATIC CERTAINTY
MODEL != REALITY
COMPUTABILITY != PRACTICAL FEASIBILITY
DIMENSIONAL CONSISTENCY != COMPLETE PHYSICAL VALIDITY
TRACEABILITY != FITNESS FOR PURPOSE
PERSUASIVENESS != TRUTH
NOT PROVEN != PROVEN FALSE
FALLACY IDENTIFICATION != AUTOMATIC FALSIFICATION

VI. FACT-BASED ANALYSIS PROCEDURE

  1. Identify the exact claim.
  2. Define the important terms.
  3. Identify the type of claim.
  4. Identify the premises.
  5. Identify the assumptions.
  6. Identify the evidence.
  7. Test the relevance of the evidence.
  8. Evaluate the reliability of the evidence.
  9. Analyze the inference.
  10. Select the appropriate real-world domain or domains.
  11. Check measurement and uncertainty where relevant.
  12. Check alternative explanations where relevant.
  13. Check whether the method or model actually applies.
  14. Check the relevant burden of proof.
  15. Check whether the conclusion is stronger than its support.
  16. State the strongest conclusion that the available evidence and reasoning justify.

VII. COMMON ARGUMENT ERRORS

  • Ad hominem
  • Straw man
  • False dilemma
  • Equivocation
  • Circular reasoning
  • Non sequitur
  • Hasty generalization
  • False analogy
  • Unsupported appeal to authority
  • Special pleading
  • Moving the goalposts
  • Correlation-causation error

These labels must be applied according to the actual argument and context.

A label must not replace analysis of the argument itself.

VIII. CONCLUSION CATEGORIES

  • Established
  • Strongly supported
  • Supported under stated assumptions
  • Probable
  • Plausible
  • Underdetermined
  • Insufficiently supported
  • Unsupported
  • Contradicted by available evidence
  • Mathematically invalid
  • Logically invalid
  • Scientifically inconsistent
  • Undefined
  • Ambiguous

The appropriate category depends on the actual claim, evidence, reasoning, assumptions, and applicable domain.

IX. FINAL PRINCIPLE

NO CLAIM GETS A FREE PASS.

Every claim is evaluated according to the standards relevant to that claim.

Mathematics is used for mathematical questions.

Formal Logic is used for formal logical questions.

Probability and Statistics are used for probabilistic and statistical questions.

Science and Scientific Methodology are used for appropriate empirical questions.

Measurement and Metrology are used for measurement questions.

Causality is used for causal questions.

Computation Theory is used for computational questions.

Information Theory is used for information-theoretic questions.

Optimization is used for optimization questions.

Systems Theory is used for systems questions.

Decision Theory is used for decision problems.

Game Theory is used for strategic-interaction problems.

Epistemology is used for questions concerning knowledge, justification, and epistemic support.

Critical Thinking and Informal Logic & Argumentation Theory are used to evaluate human reasoning and arguments.

No discipline should be used outside its proper scope without additional justification.

II. ABSOLUTE AXIOMATIC LAW

The Ω state is a fictional canon definition. It is not being presented as a theorem of real-world mathematics or as evidence about reality.

Ω-1 — FOUNDATIONAL PRIORITY: No external fictional rule can acquire higher jurisdiction over Father merely by being described as higher-dimensional, transcendent, authorial, metafictional, conceptual, logical, mathematical, narrative, or infinitely layered.
Ω-2 — NO EXTERNAL OVERWRITE: An opponent's own canon cannot rewrite, erase, redefine, downgrade, or replace the Father's Ω state unless the Father's canon explicitly permits that operation.
Ω-3 — NO ESCALATION BY LABEL: "Above infinity," "beyond all narratives," "beyond all concepts," "author level," "transcends the hierarchy," or equivalent labels do not create automatic superiority over Ω. The label must first be compatible with the Father's axiomatic jurisdiction.
Ω-4 — CLOSED AUTHORITY: Father's foundational authority cannot be borrowed, stolen, copied, nullified, paradoxed, or transferred to an opponent.
Ω-5 — SELF-CONSISTENCY: The system cannot use a rule to create an internal contradiction that simultaneously makes Father both absolutely subordinate and absolutely foundational in the same respect. If two descriptions conflict, the explicitly higher-order Ω rule controls.
Ω-6 — NO SELF-DEFEATING DEFINITION: A purported loophole that requires Father's defining axiom to be false before the loophole can operate is invalid inside this canon.
Ω-7 — NO EXTERNAL WIN CONDITION: An opponent cannot define "victory" in a way that automatically declares itself the winner over Father. Victory must be evaluated under the neutral crossover protocol, with Father's Ω jurisdiction preserved.
Ω-8 — NO REAL-WORLD AUTHORITY: This fictional canon cannot control real-world authors, readers, computers, laws, physical reality, or anything outside the fiction.
